Traditional statistical models, including HDTM, typically rely on the assumption that data is randomly selected from a given distribution, however in the context of information networks this assumption is often violated. Existing solutions to classification tasks in networks rely on graph-based neural models that produce favorable performance when tested. However, in this study, we investigate the potential of utilizing an unsupervised statistical model to improve classification of network nodes. By leveraging a comprehensive dataset consisting of twelve domains covering social media, online forums, and academic content, we compare the performance of HDTM and deep neural models on the INAC task. Our results indicate that the Hierarchical Document Topic Model, enhanced with node attributes when applicable, outperforms graph-based neural models on ten of the twelve tested domains.

Researchers examined the final escape states of linear three-body scattering systems, consisting of two heavy particles and one lighter particle, in a set-up where the lighter particle initiated the collision with the other two, forming an equilateral triangle configuration. Their analysis focused on the much lighter particle escaping much farther than the other two, leading to a an asymmetric momentum distribution, with a long tail, resembling that of a power-law. This long-tailed effect was consistently observed across various calculations, using three-body scattering amplitudes with varying levels of complexity, all of which were based on the effective field theory called 'Light' [1]. The calculations also enabled the reproduction of two-body scattering data with high accuracy, according to existing measurements. The emergence of power-law long-tailed patterns in three-body scattering events has not been seen before in similar studies, even with the lighter particle having a much smaller momentum than the other two, down to a certain point where it carried at least a tenth of the other particles' momentum.

The nuclear modification factors of prompt $\psi$(2S) and J/$\psi$ mesons were determined in p-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, based on the full data set reported earlier. Examinations of the nuclear dependence on the transverse momentum and the rapidity domain were conducted, and the findings showed a consistent pattern of suppression in the transverse momentum range of 3-50 GeV/$c$, with a slightly increased suppression occurring at lower transverse momenta for $\psi$(2S) compared to J/$\psi$. Additionally, the ratio of $\psi$(2S) over J/$\psi$ was calculated as a function of transverse momentum and found to exhibit significant variations.

This paper explores a specific concept of equivalence relation in the context of continuous logic and proves its association with complete metric spaces, as well as an alternative representation using uniform spaces. Additionally, it defines the idea of a quotient space and establishes the relationship between equivalence relations and the generation of new theories in the language. Furthermore, it investigates the properties of equivalence relations in the context of model theory.

This research proposes an innovative approach that leverages dimensional reduction techniques to identify the core aspects of software configurations undergoing changes. By applying the principles of singular value decomposition to configure datasets, this method effectively filters out minor variations and highlights the significant differences. As a proof-of-concept, this approach has been effectively applied to software evolution analysis of 12 prominent Java frameworks, showcasing its capability to accurately pinpoint the core features changing configurations. Additionally, this method has been used to analyze the impact of dependencies on software project workflows.

Deep learning methods that employ recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have achieved significant success across various sequence-based tasks. Nevertheless, tackling long-form sequences still poses a challenge due to the propagation of errors throughout the sequence. This issue can be addressed by utilizing attention mechanisms within deep sequential models, which selectively emphasize particular sequence elements to facilitate better understanding and outcome prediction. However, the task of learning relevant sequence representations remains intricate, and the quality heavily relies on the design of attention mechanisms. This study investigates the effectiveness of novel attention schemes that prioritize elements based on their relative distance from the current processing point, either by favoring those that come next (forward attention) or those that come before (backward attention). The proposed forward attention mechanism mimics the attention process in human cognition, focusing on the most critical details at any given time. The backward attention mechanism, on the other hand, mimics the eye movements during reading tasks. The study provides an in-depth analysis of these mechanisms' behavior and their comparison with established methods on three benchmark datasets. The results reveal that both novel attention mechanisms yield comparable or even better performance than established methods.

Cassiopeia A's X-ray emission exhibits a significant polarization of 10% at 5 keV, showing a symmetrical distribution around 90 degrees. This finding contradicts radio observations suggesting the South Pole Tibeta's magnetic field is aligned with the neutron star's magnetic axis. The observed polarization angle in X-rays is 30 degrees away from the predicted angle based on radio data. It is proposed that the difference stems from a misinterpretation of the neutron star's magnetic field shape. Alternatively, it is proposed that the X-ray emission originates from a region close to the jet base where the magnetic field's shape is distorted due to jet formation.

The minimum number of elements to choose from a set of $n$ to ensure that the sums from subsets of those elements are distinct, all having a size of less than or equal to $\alpha n$ for some $0\le\alpha\le 1$, is investigated here. In cases where $\alpha$ approaches 1, classic results from Diophantine geometry apply and the required number of elements grows in direct proportion to the total count. However, as the value of $\alpha$ decreases below $\frac12$, significantly distinct, often non-intuitive, lower bounds can be found. Our most recent findings even offer a solution to multi-dimensional variant known as the distinct subset sum problem for vectors and provide a simplified explanation for the long-standing Hilbert's 10th problem in the context of commutative algebra.

This study explores the connection between the presence of a deconfinement phase transition and the properties of quark stars, specifically those comprising uniformly rotating objects. To achieve this, we employ a modified version of the MIT bag model, applied to both spherical and rotating quark star models. Our analysis focuses on the impact of phase transitions on mass, radius, and rotation rate for each star type. Our results indicate that the mass of a star that experiences a deconfinement transition is lower than one that doesn't, and the difference increases with the star's angular velocity. Additionally, we find that considering rotation has a greater effect on the properties of stars that undergo a deconfinement transition than those that don't.

The goal of this research is to validate the effectiveness of a novel method for extracting information from the compass system's output, which utilizes the properties of the compass state to estimate the damping parameters in an optical levitation setup. The study employs the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound to assess the precision limits of the estimated parameters, based on analytical calculations of the compass state statistics. The outcomes are compared with simulation results, verifying that increasing the number of measurements in the compass can enhance the precision of the estimated parameters, although the improvements diminish as the number of measurements rises. Furthermore, this work investigates how the characteristics of the compass can be modified to enhance the precision of the estimated parameters, highlighting the potential of the method in enhancing optical levitation technology.

Our method extracts the unique shape features of individual liquid jets within an airflow by analyzing time-resolved images.  The approach involves determining the unique characteristics (geometry) of each jet through the application of a clustering algorithm to time-resolved images, taken at regular intervals, in an airflow.  The formation of the recirculation zone and the oscillations of the jet can be tracked over time, and the successful identification of the jet geometry has been confirmed by comparing it with manually extracted features.  This method offers potential applications in distinguishing between different shapes of particles, such as those produced by electro-spinning processes.

The adhesion between viruses and host cells is a critical initial step in infection that has been extensively researched through computer simulations. Unlike red blood cells, which are rigid and simple in shape, other cells are complex and dynamic. To simulate viral attachment to these cells, a complex model is required. In this study, a novel flexible cell framework called 'CellSurface' was created using the Chombo library to complexly represent cell surfaces. By viewing a cell as a collection of two-dimensional surfaces, the model allows for the simulation of delicate processes such as viral binding, cell movement, and immune system reactions. A novel viral movement mechanism "metabolic flow" was also developed, enabling realistic movements between a virus and its environment. For example, when a virus encounters a cell, it can roll along its surface before being internalized. The model was tested using a VHH virus binding to a pseudotype of the CD4 receptor found on T cells. As a novel system for simulating viral attachment to complex cells, the CellSurface framework provides a platform for exploring a wide range of complex biological interactions.

Our investigation into the origins of warped galaxies focuses on the environmental influences that affect their shape. We are the first to thoroughly examine how a galaxy's surrounding affects its own morphology using detailed simulations. Our study reveals distinct differences in how a galaxy's shape is affected by its surroundings in S and U type galaxies. We found that an U type galaxy is generally more susceptible to tides and galaxy interactions. Notably, in an S type galaxy, a contributing factor to warping is often the galactic bulge. We discovered that an S type galaxy tends to maintain its warped structure over billions of years, whereas a U type galaxy is more likely to experience a complete restoration of its disk shape. We propose that the difference in warping mechanisms could lead to a distinction in the types of stars each galaxy possesses. The implications of our findings suggest that an S type galaxy is more likely to be found in a peaceful, isolated environment, whereas a U type galaxy is more likely to be part of a larger galaxy cluster, engaged in frequent interactions with its neighboring galaxies.

This paper employs a growth criterion for harmonic functions to the effect that 
their growth dimension is limited to $n + \frac{Q}{2}$, where $n$ represents 
the dimension of the space, $Q$ denotes the fractional Q-curvature, and this 
growth dimension cannot exceed $n + 1$ when $Q = 0$. Building on this growth 
framework, we derive precise bounds for the growth dimension of $p$-harmonic 
functions (with $p \neq 2$) in the context of $p$-Laplacian Ricci solitons.

This study employs a computational method to investigate the structural properties and
semiconducting behavior of binary A$_2$B$_4$ compounds, specifically focusing on potassium-rubidium-bismuth and potassium-caesium-bismuth under various levels of doping.
Within the framework of density functional theory and the generalized gradient approximation,
we determine the most stable crystalline structures of these substances and model different
Dopant configurations in a supercell.
By utilizing a semiempirical functional to describe electron correlations, we're able to
improve the accuracy of calculated band gaps.
Results indicate a direct band gap for undoped potassium-rubidium-bismuth and a indirect
band gap for undoped potassium-caesium-bismium; both become direct with appropriate doping.
Doping either rubidium or caesium into potassium-rubidium-bismuth and potassium-caesium-bismium leads to a contraction along the a and b axes and an expansion along the c axis, with significant changes to their electronic structures and stability in relation to the doping concentration.

The impact of electron phonon coupling on the polarization oscillations in metals and insulators is examined, particularly how it varies with temperature.  The study focuses on the second-order electrostatic response, accounting for both adiabatic and non-adibatic contributions.  In adiabatic conditions, the non-stochastic component of the Born effective charge is zero in perfect conductors and insulators, whereas it equals the standard Born charge only in the adiabatic approximation for the insulator.  In the non-adibatic case, the total Born effective charge is calculated within the local density approximation for several materials, showing significant deviations from the standard values in some cases.  The work also introduces a novel approach to determine the non-adibatic Born effective charge through time-dependent density functional calculations, particularly applicable to metals.  The derived model includes both adiabatic and non-adibatic components, enabling separate identification and comparison with experimental data.

This research expands upon the fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation (FNS) previously proposed in the 90's by by E and Goldman to model turbulence, and recent extensions by by by E, Goldman and by by by E, by developing a mathematical framework that establishes the FNS as a stochastic differential law with a deterministic force, and thereby confirms the hypothesis that the FNS is statistically equivalent to the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation (NSE) at large scales. In contrast to earlier studies that relied on specific assumptions about the noise characteristics, this work derives the equivalence more broadly, and also demonstrates that the sum of a deterministic force and a white noise force can effectively reproduce the statistics of a real-time turbulent flow measured experimentally. As a consequence, this research opens up new avenues for the design of artificial swimmers based on a deterministic force, and also suggests a novel method for solving the inverse problem of determining the deterministic force acting within a turbulent flow.

The Witten effect asserts that in $U(1)$ gauge theory with $N_f$ WISPs (Weakly Interacting Scalar Particles) as Higgs, a magnetic monopole induces a Dirac gap. This notion has been expanded to include general non-Abelian gauge theories and multiple types of WISPs. Our research examines the validity of the Witten effect in the context of $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetry and three-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ super Yang-Mills theory coupled with fundamental scalars. The findings show that the Witten effect emerges when the monopole operator creates holonomy in scalar fields, resulting in a Dirac gap. This is supported by a holographic model of three-dimensional theory.

This work examines a class of nonlinear delay systems characterized by their sensitivity to small perturbations in their parameters, leading to complex dynamics. However, these systems can be simplified by considering an approach that treats parameter variations as part of the system's dynamics, effectively reducing the effective dimensionality. This approach relies on the concept of enhanced diffusion to establish a lower bound on the system's embedding dimension. Through theoretical and numerical analysis of two model systems, we demonstrate the validity of this method and illustrate the system's behavior under varying parameter conditions.

This paper compares the denotational and operational definitions of higher-order probabilistic functional programs developed in the small-step operational semantics framework.  Initially, denotational and operational interpretations of continuous-type programs are explored, focusing on the connectivity of a probabilistic version of PCF known as pPCF_C.  A recent study by Ong and Yuen, which established a denotational-to-operational correspondence for a probabilistic version of PCF (pPCF_B) with Borel-type programs, is also reviewed.  Building on this prior work, a probabilistic version of PCF with a dependent type system (pPCF_D) is introduced and both denotational and operational methodologies are applied to investigate the semantics of high-order probabilistic functional programs.  In contrast to the denotational and operational approaches for Borel-type and continuous-type programs, the denotational and operational definitions for pPCD fail to cohere.

This paper investigates design-mining tasks that involve predicting conclusions from multiple product descriptions. In the field of text classification, various techniques can be employed to address this challenge. To gauge their effectiveness, our study evaluates several design-mining conclusions across multiple product categories from research platforms with a substantial number of papers. The outcomes reveal that utilizing multiple-conclusion classifiers and incorporating external knowledge through NLP techniques enhances the stability of conclusion predictions and improves the relevance of design-mining outcomes.

In this work, we investigate the de Sitter universe model with holographic dark energy (HDE) and modify the Ricci-Schwarz power-law model by using a scalar field coupled with a polynomial potential. We assume the HDE universe horizon represents the boundary of the universe, and this is related to the effective fluid's vacuum energy (cosmological constant $\Lambda$) through the Einstein equations, which can be interpreted as a result of the dark vacuum energy possessing negative pressure. We examine the exponential and polynomial types of polynomial potentials. Firstly, considering the exponential potential, we find the best-fitting results for the exponent $\alpha$ and coupling constant $\xi$ using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sensitivity analysis, assuming a flat universe with age constraints. Secondly, for the polynomial potential of degree two, we perform similar analyses but with different parameters ($\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, and $\xi$). However, these results indicate that the parameters of the polynomial potential lack physical significance due to the lack of a clear minimum for the scalar field. Consequently, this implies that the model is not suitable for cosmological analysis.

This research presents an efficient approach to accelerate optimization procedures by pinpointing the distinctive structures within the loss landscape of a given function. By identifying the underlying differentiability manifold of a smooth loss, we significantly boost the convergence rate of various optimization methods, including stochastic gradient descent, to achieve a faster $O(1/K)$ convergence, similar to what is seen with non-stochastic nonconvex optimization algorithms. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of optimization procedures, such as adaptive gradient methods and second-order techniques, resulting in improved performance in both simulated and real-world data settings. We validate the efficacy of our novel algorithm through comprehensive numerical experiments that demonstrate substantial acceleration compared to traditional methods.

This paper explores various aspects of the cube of a weakly 1-absorbing prime ideal in the context of Riemannian nilpotent algebras, specifically focusing on prime and 1-absorbing ideals within these structures. Key findings include a characterization of the prime ideals whose cube is also prime, as well as a characterization of the weakly 1-absorbing prime ideals whose cube is not 1-absorbing. Furthermore, the paper establishes a connection between the nilpotent length of an algebra and the number of generators required for its cube to be a semiprime ideal.

A statistical method is described to integrate experimental data from several sources for the purpose of determining branching fractions of certain decay processes involving the $\chi$ mesons. The method is used to calculate the branching fractions of $\chi(1S)$ decays into kaons and electrons, and is also applied to $\chi(2P)$ decays into either kaons and electrons or muons and electrons. The primary source of uncertainty in these calculations is the uncertainty associated with the production rates of the $\chi$ mesons themselves.

Measuring the angular distribution of light sources is a fundamental aspect of
astrophysics, with such measurements commonly employed in mammalian
vision--involving cells like the retina and the brain functioning together as
an efficient image-processing system. Similarities between these biological
systems and modern telescopes exist, with both being used to study the universe.
In our study, a novel, lightweight image processing technique is introduced to
calculate the angular distribution in wide-field astrophysics, accounting for
non-uniform pixel sensitivity and accounting for time delays between pixels. By
doing so, we demonstrate that this approach can contribute to groundbreaking
astrophysical observations, including the measurement of bi-isotropic correlation
lags in diffuse sources. Furthermore, this technique shows potential in other
fields such as high-energy physics and defense, due to its ability to be adapted
into portable and lightweight devices.

In pharmacology, accurate relational machine learning models are crucial for making informed decisions about drug development and approval. To assess their reliability, it is essential to evaluate these models using diverse datasets, differing from the standard training sets. This paper investigates the performance of relational machine learning models on a dataset of pharmacological target properties called TOX4, which was created with the aim of promoting transparency in model training processes. By analyzing the results, we found that these models exhibit significant predictions discrepancies when applied to targets not included in their training, yet still claim high overall accuracy rates. Furthermore, we identify the need for more open pharmacological datasets, akin to ImageNet, to facilitate fair model comparisons and assessments.

Many countries lack a comprehensive and updated assessment of their road conditions.
Utilizing crowdsourced data from vehicles has shown potential in monitoring road conditions.
This study leverages a smartphone's built-in sensors to capture road condition information.
A vehicle can act as a mobile data collector, gathering information about the road it's traversing.
Through experimentation, we found that a smartphone's accelerometer and GPS can effectively
predict road conditions, such as surface type and quality. A machine learning model was developed
to analyze the gathered data, providing a solution to monitor road conditions autonomously.
Moreover, our approach offers a cost-effective solution with minimal implementation and maintenance costs.

Learning policies from expert demonstrations without explicit knowledge of the expert's environment is a key goal in imitation learning.  To achieve this goal, current methods rely on comparing the agent's observations to the expert's observations, assuming they share the same sensory inputs.  However, differing sensor configurations, data preprocessing methods, or bugs in the provided data can create significant discrepancies between the two environments.  If left unaddressed, these discrepancies can hinder learning or cause the agent to learn from irrelevant aspects.  In this paper, we identify these discrepancies as a challenge to imitation learning and propose a framework to disentangle them.  By separating the underlying state and observations from a random and noisy component, our approach enables agents to filter out irrelevant information and learn a policy that is less susceptible to systematic differences.  Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on various tasks, including a customized Algenbox experiment and a real-world dataset derived from MuJoCo.

We investigate how protostar formation is influenced by a collapsing gas cloud's angular momentum and how it leads to the formation of a disk. To examine this influence, we simulate the collapse of rotating gas clouds in a laboratory set-up using lasers and particles and compare the results to theoretical models of star formation. We focus specifically on the process of protostar and disk formation because the cloud's angular momentum plays a significant role in this process. When a cloud with substantial angular momentum collapses, it undergoes disk fragmentation, which hinders the formation of a single protostar. However, our laboratory experiments and simulations show that increasing the cloud's angular momentum beyond a certain threshold can actually cause the disk to oscillate violently, ultimately preventing the formation of a protostar. We observe the formation of protostars in clouds with lower angular momentum but find that a protostar's mass is directly proportional to the cloud's angular momentum. This relationship suggests that the cloud's oscillations due to rotation actually contribute to protostar formation. This finding has significant implications for understanding the protostar formation process and its relationship to the cloud's angular momentum.

This research focuses on the logical foundations of association rule discovery. By leveraging lattice theory, the paper formalizes the notion of redundancy among association rules using logical entailment and provides a method to characterize and eliminate such rules from a dataset. This research enhances our understanding of the relationships between association rules and provides a theoretical framework for existing algorithms designed to remove redundant rules from datasets.

Individuals struggling with mental health issues are overrepresented in the criminal justice system, yet receiving insufficient intervention. To tackle this issue, researchers examined the potential of using medical treatment to reduce criminal recidivism rates. By applying causal discovery methods to a dataset combining crime data and mental health treatments, along with a selection of patients suffering from specific conditions, along with their prosecution records, they aimed to identify the most effective treatments for particular crimes and patients. Their study demonstrated that, in comparison to patients not receiving treatment, patients receiving inpatient or outpatient therapy exhibited decreased criminal activity following treatment, especially for less violent crimes. Certain therapeutic approaches were also found to be more successful at reducing specific types of crime, providing valuable insights that can direct the allocation of limited resources within the justice and health systems.

This paper employs complex analysis methods to derive a family of special polynomials, 
namely Sheffer polynomials, by utilizing generating functions. We examine key properties 
of these polynomials and establish a precise relationship between their generating functions 
and reproducing kernels. We also explore duality between polynomials and power series, 
identifying the significant roles of inverse operators and complementary sequences in this 
connection. To illustrate our findings, we revisit several well-known examples of Sheffer polynomials, 
and employ our results to define new families of orthogonal polynomials related to stochastic processes.

Creating accurate radio maps is a complex task that necessitates a substantial amount of signal measurements collected from various locations. Since the measurement process can be costly and time-consuming, effectively gathering the most informative data possible is crucial. This paper introduces a new metric for quantifying the uncertainty of radio maps and utilizes it to guide a measurement selection process that optimizes the collection of the most informative data possible. The proposed metric is based on a widely-established statistical framework and can be efficiently computed with a simplified, stable algorithm. Furthermore, this metric is utilized in a series of optimization problems that address different scenarios, such as selectively gathering measurements from a limited number of locations and expanding a radio map by incorporating new measurements. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in identifying the most informative data for refining the maps.

One of the key benefits of unsupervised learning is its ability to identify irregularities in data without human labeling, a process that can be both time-consuming and costly. Anomaly detection, a crucial area of study in this context, is focused on identifying unusual patterns in data that deviate from the standard. One effective method for detecting anomalies involves using generative adversarial networks (GANs), particularly Anomaly GAN (AlGAN), which is capable of identifying rare data by learning from both normal and abnormal samples. However, the performance of AlGAN is heavily dependent on the type of datasets it is applied to and often struggles with identifying genuine anomalies in small datasets. In this research, a modified version of the traditional cross-entropy loss used in training GANs is introduced to improve the performance of AnGAN on small datasets. Additionally, the impact of varying the loss function is investigated to determine its effect on the ability of AlGAN models to identify rare data. An extensive analysis of the results from these experiments reveals that the traditional cross-entropy loss is more effective than its alternative in identifying genuine anomalies and also addresses a limitation in the current approach to training GANs that contributes to their ability to identify irregularities in data.

This paper evaluates the effectiveness of multiple verification systems in identifying offline handwritten signatures under both clean and real-world scenarios. A new dataset, MoSig2, featuring 999 signature trails from 99 individuals, has been created with a built-in testing framework. Signature samples in this dataset have been obtained from the MoSig challenge participants' signatures, provided nearly a decade ago. Three verification methods, previously applied in the first competition round, are examined and compared. Their performances are assessed using the widely recognized EER and WRCC error measures. When testing on the clean MoSig2 instances, the original systems demonstrated consistent results similar to those seen in the competition. Nonetheless, under noisy conditions, notable discrepancies were observed between the original approaches and those re-implemented from competition submissions.

This study investigates the efficacy of various data augmentation methods in advanced language models for sourcing additional training examples. We examine how six different augmentation techniques enhance a base model's performance, and find that some techniques are more beneficial than others. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the effectiveness of these techniques is highly dependent on the amount of original training data available. For instance, SOTA performance improvements can be substantial - up to 2.5% - when training data is limited to 512 tokens. However, this method provides negligible benefits when training on 2048 tokens. We also introduce a simple and efficient approach called Rapid Alternating Self-conditioning to mitigate the issues associated with long training sequences, which can be applied to other models such as LM, GM, and GM-LM with gradient matching and language matching.

This research investigates how the Galerkin method in neutron transport theory corresponds to maximum likelihood estimation. Initially, a simplified neutron transport model is explored. Utilizing non-homogeneous discrete-neutron density functions as model parameters, variations in these functions are defined. An objective function representing the mean squared residual is formulated, and its minimum, which corresponds to the maximum likelihood, is found using the Galerkin method. By establishing the consistency of the method and its convergence under certain conditions, weak convergence is shown. A numerical example utilizing a grid-based approach demonstrates the convergence of the method, even when the parameter space is not compact. Building on this foundation, a more complex zero-energy time-dependent neutron transport problem with 6 groups of discrete energies is tackled. The research successfully employs the Galerkin method to estimate the parameters of the problem, which involves various macroscopic parameters such as cross-sections, leakage terms, and fission rates. The findings, including critical thresholds and damage estimates, are then compared with the actual values.

The growing demand for analyzing large datasets has led to a significant increase in the development of sophisticated data management systems that support sophisticated queries and provide robust protection against privacy threats. The current methods of maintaining data privacy in data management systems are primarily centered on individual data records, disregarding the intricate connections between records, which are essential for comprehending certain phenomena. The omission of these connections may lead to unintended privacy breaches. The proposed work aims to bridge this gap by introducing a novel framework that incorporates inter-record relationships into the framework. The proposed framework leverages graph theory to model the relationships between records and utilizes the concept of gradient masking and perturbing to maintain privacy. The development of this framework involves defining new notions of privacy breaches and applying optimization techniques to minimize the cost of maintaining privacy while maximizing data accuracy. The practical applicability of the proposed framework is demonstrated through an empirical study on synthetic data sets.

Our study utilizes the EHTC and ALMA telescopes to observe the disk around the PDS 70 system at separate distances from its star, specifically at 20-30 au and 70-100 au, using the molecules C$_2$H and CO. We discovered that the C$_2$H column density in the outer region is significantly lower than in the inner region, and this difference is attributed to C$_2$H's reaction with forming grains. In areas where the C/O elemental ratio is elevated, such as in the outer region, C$_2$H is converted into CH$_2$OH radicals, while in areas with lower C/O ratios, such as in the inner region, C$_2$H forms more readily. We found a correlation between C$_2$ H and CO column densities in both observed areas, and this is thought to indicate that the disks' gas and solid dust components originate from the same source material. Additionally, our research reveals that the emission from the C$_2$H molecule in the inner region is more concentrated and localized compared to the CO molecule, and this is believed to indicate that C$_2$ H plays a key role in the formation of small solid particles in the proximity of the star.

Analyzing large datasets, particularly those resulting from astrophysics research, can be a time-consuming and labor-intensive process with current tools. The Extensible Time-tag Analyzer offers a faster and more efficient alternative to existing software, supporting a broader range of data formats and enabling the creation of custom analysis pipelines with an intuitive graphical interface. By allowing researchers to construct and edit analysis pipelines without needing to write code, ETA makes it easy to adapt to new data formats as they are developed, giving researchers more control over their data and computations.

Mean field games offer a framework for analyzing large systems where numerous agents interact with each other, and equilibrium existence is a critical concept within this context. However, introducing regularity requirements can significantly impact the ability to find an equilibrium, as observed in our current research. We demonstrate that under weak assumptions - necessary for stochastic differential equations to have solutions - no equilibrium may exist in mean field games. This finding stands despite numerous methods developed to prove equilibrium existence. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the lack of equilibrium is directly linked to systems in which no regular flow is present. To address this challenge, we suggest a new approach, which provides a method for constructing a sequence of approximations leading to the existence of an equilibrium in a smaller system with reduced player interactions.

Our research involves analyzing the chemical composition of nine metal-poor stellar systems in the Galaxy, utilizing a large sample of 3077 low-mass subgiant stars spanning from 50 pc to 10 kpc in radius. We assessed chemical abundance for six key elements (Al, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti, and Fe) and compared it to local field stars to investigate chemical uniformity and potential patterns across distant regions. We discovered modest variations in abundance among distant stellar groups (-0.15 dex to 0.20 dex) relative to local fields, with no evident correlation between distance and chemical composition. Furthermore, we found no substantial differences between distant stellar groups and local fields in terms of spread or skewness. Notably, our results from analyzing elemental ratios in distant stellar groups align with the findings from studying metal-poor stars at high latitudes, suggesting that these regions share a shared origin and that their chemical composition was formed solely through rapid iron enrichment.

The fast growth of the sharing economy and the increasing popularity of renting out unique items create opportunities for reducing fashion waste. To enhance the user experience in creating outfits with shared items, it's crucial to flag potential mismatches as early as possible. To tackle this challenge, we developed a novel approach that combines image processing and learning techniques to improve detecting mismatched items in custom outfits. Notably, existing research primarily focuses on image segmentation, but these methods fall short when dealing with user-created outfits containing diverse and uncommon items. In contrast, we propose using hand-crafted features and neural networks specifically designed for early detection, yielding a recall of 0.91 and precision of 0.99 on a dataset of 500 outfits, comprising 13,610 images.

In the past ten years, there has been significant growth in the field of non-classical resource theories, driven in part by the potential for quantum information theories to improve existing technologies. Non-classical resource theories have wide-ranging applications, including helping to understand the fundamental principles of nature and developing more secure communication systems. The past decade has seen notable advancements in this field, characterized by the analysis of entanglement-based resources, non-markovian dynamics, quantum coherence, and non-locality. The impact of non-classical resource theories can be seen in numerous breakthroughs, and this overview will highlight some of the most significant developments of the past decade, while also looking ahead to potential future advancements in this field.

Enhancing the scalability of federated learning in complex applications is a difficult task, mainly due to the current FL frameworks' inability to efficiently manage a large number of users and tests. A key issue here is the protection of user data, as existing FL frameworks typically require the exchange of raw data with the central server, thus compromising this privacy. A new algorithm called FedBuff is proposed to improve the scalability of FL while maintaining user privacy through data encryption. FedBuff operates by converting encrypted data into fixed-size buffer areas on the server and locally on each user's device. This buffer area is then used to perform local averaging on the encrypted data. Upon aggregation, the server uses the Adam optimizer with stochastic gradient descent for model updates, a process facilitated by the encrypted, quantized gradients. As a result, FedBuff eliminates the need for raw data exchange and achieves significant time and cost savings in large-scale FL experiments.

Our goal is to establish a Banach algebra calculus for polynomial shift semigroups and determine its properties, including the nature of its dual and commutant. We demonstrate that the commutant is equivalent to the algebra itself when the semigroup is not a homomorphism, and find that its dual is isometric to its commutant when it acts on a specific subspace of the Bohr compactification of the torus.

The existence of dark matter continues to be a puzzle in contemporary cosmology. Primordial black holes (PBPs) provide a potential solution as completely invisible matter. Recent research suggests that a specific range of PBPs having masses from $10^{-12}$ to $10^{-9}$ solar masses, which constitute a substantial portion of dark matter, are created during the collapse of dark matter-dominated mini-halos. We investigate the impact of core collapse on the predicted PBPs through 3D N-body simulations. As a result, we discover that the PBPs formed through the collapse of dark matter-dominated mini-halos significantly decrease. This outcome indicates that the standard model of core collapse should be reconsidered when calculating PBP production.

Our previous computer simulations of a particle raft under turbulent fluid flow revealed the development of interfacial structures similar to those observed in experiments. To gain a deeper understanding of these findings, we conducted additional simulations using a larger domain to collect detailed information about the fluid and particle movements. These new results confirm the occurrence of the re-aggregation of particles away from the interface and the expansion of the fluid in the vicinity of the raft. A theoretical analysis suggests that the competition between re-aggregation and fluid expansion leads to a specific pattern of rift formation. A longer duration of our simulations allowed us to collect statistics on the movement of individual particles within the raft and the characteristics of its surface. In contrast to earlier simulations, our new data show that particles can move freely throughout the raft when the applied stress is sub-critical. A comparison between our findings and experimental data reveals significant agreement. A longer duration of our simulations in the vicinity of the interface allowed us to collect more precise information about the formation of rifts and their scaling. Our new results show that the scaling of rifts depends on the time since their creation and the level of applied stress. A description of the observed phenomena suggests that they are related to a transition in the behavior of the raft from a solid-like to a fluid-like state.

The gallium nitride material properties can be improved by matching its lattice to magnesium gallium spinel compounds, specifically MgSiN$_2$ and MgGeN$_2$. Our study discovered that substituting silicon or germanium for oxygen in these compounds results in a room-temperature hole mobility of up to 100 cm$^2$/V/s in gallium nitride, significantly higher than the 1 cm$^2$/V/s achieved through conventional means. Moreover, both ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$ exhibit high carrier concentrations with magnitudes exceeding 10$^{19}$ per cm$^3$. The electronic properties of these materials are modulated by small adjustments to the oxygen content and then annealed to attain stable and reproducible results. The ultimate potential of these materials lies in their integration into lattice-matched gallium nitride templates for advanced power electronics applications.

Sparse policy gradient methods are susceptible to sparse gradient approximations, which can be challenging to apply in complex environments. This work proposes SPGP-SARSA, a novel sparse policy gradient algorithm based on a value function-based approach for policy evaluation. Theoretical analysis reveals that SPGP-SARSA achieves a faster convergence rate than existing sparse gradient methods in certain scenarios. The performance of SPGP-SARSA is evaluated in underwater navigation tasks and compared with a range of algorithms.

This paper introduces a method to create new isothermic surfaces by applying
M\"obius and Crulli transformations to simply connected patches. We demonstrate
how to derive the isothermic equation for the composition of these transformations
and discuss the conditions under which the resulting surfaces remain isothermic.

This study introduces a novel, kernel-based method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) that does not require the assumption of a parametric model. It utilizes a stochastic dimension reduction method with kernel-based interpolation, ensuring the resulting operator is non-smooth due to the nature of kernel dependencies. The approach can be applied to various problems that are too complex for traditional projection techniques like Galerkin methods. Our method has the advantage of being more robust to noise and model errors. However, the smooth approximation of the operator enables the use of limiting techniques to obtain a continuous solution. Our method's performance is evaluated on high-dimensional PDEs with numerous variables, and the results are compared to other techniques.

This research paper delves into projective recurrence relations associated with modified Dowling polynomials, a group of homogeneous polynomials that can be seen as extensions of classical Dowling polynomials. These modified polynomials arise from combining a parameter $\lambda$ with the parameters $m_1, \ldots, m_k$, which can be negative. We derive a projective recurrence relation using the $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and show that previously published formulas for $x_1^n y_1^{nm_1} \cdots y_k^{nm_k}$ representations of $\lambda$-analogues match our derived recurrence formulas.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking idea for creating temporal knowledge graph embeddings that outperforms existing models. The proposed method, called REFARE, addresses two key issues in temporal KGEs: the neglect of time attributes in time-aware models and the computational inefficiency of some scoring functions. REFARE addresses the first problem by incorporating time attributes into its embedding objective, demonstrating improved performance across multiple benchmark datasets. The second issue is resolved by utilizing a memory-based approach that replaces the traditional matrix multiplication used in many KGE methods, resulting in substantial speed-ups of up to 3x and 10x for our time-aware and general KGE methods, respectively, without compromising accuracy.

This note re-examines insplits and outsplits in graph theory, particularly focusing on their roles in determining strong shift equivalence. It then investigates the ideals formed by these insplits and outsplits and reveals the ring theoretic significance of the full linearisation of an graph, $Z(\Gamma)$. Furthermore, we establish the strong similarity equivalence as a powerful tool for creating strong shift equivalents from graphs containing insplits or outsplits. Additionally, we address the issue of unique strong shift equivalents for graphs without redundant edges.

To analyze the anisotropy of the heavy quark potential in 2+1 flavor QCD more deeply, we investigate the contributions beyond the lattice's straight strings, incorporating a more detailed ground state and an excited state as reference for binding energy calculations. These investigations enhance our comprehension of the heavy quark potential's anisotropy and encourage the utilization of such sophisticated approaches in the study of bound systems.

This research introduces OREO-LM, a pioneering large-scale language model that seamlessly integrates knowledge interaction into its architecture. By incorporating a knowledge interaction layer, OREO-LM's design better aligns with two core principles of knowledge-based question answering: first, a thorough understanding of the query is crucial for determining the required knowledge sources; second, the structure of the retrieved knowledge should be maintained for efficient querying. In experiments, OREO-LM consistently outperformed conventional language models, including both BERT- and FLAME-based variants, on a range of benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the proposed knowledge interaction layer enhances the accuracy of knowledge retrieval and facilitates better answering of questions by selectively leveraging the retrieved knowledge.

Currently, the best-known high dimensional expanders are achieved by the Lieb-Szwarc method.
In this research, a new, simpler way of constructing high dimensional expanders using almost Ramanujan graphs is introduced.
This new approach results in higher treedepth for a given spectral gap or a higher spectral gap for a given treedepth.
A key aspect is that this method allows us to find better group-based high dimensional expanders for any group size.
Additionally, this new construction has potential applications in other areas of computer science such as coding theory and complexity classes.

Recent advancements in language models have shown that task-agnostic training with diverse prompts can be more effective than tailored prompts for specific tasks. However, current prompt designs largely rely on expert input and are limited by the constraints of natural language syntax and semantics. Since large language models are trained on existing text data, it is plausible that unsupervised prompt design could leverage existing text to improve model performance. Our study innovates in the area of unsupervised prompt design by utilizing existing datasets to create new prompts through textual modifications. Notably, we focus on negative prompts, which are less commonly used due to concerns about model overfitting to original data. Our experiment shows that by applying simple operations such as word swapping and sentence restructuring on existing text, we can create new prompts that significantly enhance model performance on related tasks.

This essay explores connections between Hida theory and the geometry of the eigencurve, specifically for $p$-irregular representations. Some key concepts and results are examined - namely, properties of overconvergent geometry, the existence and characteristics of certain choices of regular submodules, and the relationship between Hida theory and choices of weights. The goal is to provide a self-contained introduction to this topic, with a focus on the geometric properties of the eigencurve and how they relate to the mathematics of $p$-adic theory.

To enhance the accuracy of entanglement-swapping measurements in Rydberg atom experiments, we developed a deep learning approach that efficiently processes data from multiple atoms. This method was successfully tested in a simulation involving the entanglement-swapping process, yielding reliable results even in noisy conditions equivalent to a noise level of -13 dB. Furthermore, our method outperformed conventional low-density parity-check code techniques, which were found to fail in the presence of similar levels of noise. Notably, our deep learning-based approach exhibited a substantial improvement in accuracy, amounting to a 250-fold enhancement over the LPCC method in the noise level of -13 dB.

We employ broad-line spectroscopy to examine the HII regions in UGC 8839, an allegedly quiescent spiral galaxy at a distance of 440 Mpc, claimed to possess no star-forming activity above the plane. Our study yields a diverse population of 122 HII regions spanning a wide range of distances and stellar masses. Despite UGC 8839's calm appearance, its HII region distribution exhibits a distinct disk shape and follows a standard luminosity distribution common among galaxies. Notably, a significant number of HII regions are detected in the northern and southern hemispheres at or above the plane, exceeding the expected number by a factor of 2, implying the presence of a massive halo with an extent of at least two times the extent of the plane. The presence of a vast halo and the absence of significant star-forming activity above the plane suggest a quiet, mature spiral galaxy rather than an inactive or post-starburst galaxy.

We examine the relationship between the cohomological properties and topological characteristics of the Julia set of a quasiregular self-map on a D Douady domain. Specifically, we relate certain conditions to the Hausdorff dimension of the Julia set and establish a upper bound for its Hausdorff dimension in terms of the hyperbolicity constant of the map. Moreover, we show that these results are applicable to a broad category of quasiregular mappings and utilize these findings to investigate specific examples, including theqv map on a 2-sphere and a family of hyperbolic mappings on a 3-torus.

This research uses the Mars Atmospheric Modeling Intercomparison Initiative database to study gravity waves in the Martian upper atmosphere. With a specific focus on the zonal mean, we analyzed temperature and horizontal wind speeds at altitudes ranging from 0 to 5 bar. Our findings reveal significant variations in these conditions across the entire atmosphere. Notably, at low latitudes and around 3.5 bar, we observe a sudden change in temperature, accompanied by corresponding changes in horizontal wind speeds. This phenomenon is likely caused by the sapping of the Martian atmosphere's residual energy, leading to the formation of gravity waves. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that the atmospheric flow is being controlled by a combination of thermal and momentum balance.

The production of heavy vector mesons in photon-proton and photon-nucleus collisions at the energy levels of the LHC and future colliders will be extensively studied. Due to the abundance of photons in hadronic collisions, and the favorable production conditions for these mesons, they become a preferred choice for investigation. The primary processes involved are dissociation and scattering, and to calculate the cross-sections, three-body reactions are considered. For proton-target collisions, this involves the calculation of the cross-sections for the breakup reactions $\gamma p \to V X p$, and for nucleus collisions, the calculations are spread across two cases - $\gamma p \to V X X'$ when an extra nucleon is involved, and $\gamma A \to V X A$ when the nucleus is intact. The calculations have been carried out for several vector mesons and various energy ranges, and the findings align with existing experimental data, providing a basis for anticipated measurements in future experiments.

A novel approach to audio generation is introduced by transforming the process into a problem-solving exercise, where a model identifies and addresses issues in target audio recordings to create high-quality samples. This task is facilitated by a continuous, real-time analysis of the target audio's spectral properties. A custom algorithm utilizing the STFT is applied to the audio signal, generating a sequence of critical frames that serve as input for a pre-trained diffusion model. This framework supports the creation of fixed-length audio segments, which can be extended to longer periods via segmentation and stitching techniques. Furthermore, a unique perceptual loss function leveraging the spectrogram's inherent structure improves the model's ability to focus on significant features, resulting in more accurate and engaging audio generation.

Recurrent Neural Networks offer great performance in handling sequential data but their widespread adoption is hindered by the high computational demands during training. This issue is particularly pronounced with fully connected RNNs whose computation complexity scales quadratically with the number of units and time steps. While subsequent architectures like Convolutional RNNs are more efficient they come with their own limitations such as reduced flexibility. This research introduces an innovative technique using binary structure to enhance the efficiency of binary convolutional RNNs. By applying binary quantization to both the parameters and activations as well as the internal recurrent connections, we substantially reduce the memory requirements during training. Furthermore, we develop a simple yet effective method to maintain activation precision during the backward pass via binary gradient computation. As a result, we are able to train complex binary convolutional RNNs on large datasets such as ImageNet in real-time. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed method achieves impressive results in long-term video recognition tasks while also reducing the computational costs by 30 times the original standards. The source code for this project is publicly available on GitHub.

Covid-19 vaccine rollout began in early 2021, yet the pandemic raged on, forcing policymakers to implement a new strategy of lifting moderate restrictions gradually. A crucial middle ground between disease control and economic viability has never been more crucial. A key factor is to gauge how immunization progress affects new infections in time to inform adjustments to restriction policies. Existing research often assumes a fixed infectious period but our approach uses real pandemic data to estimate the transmission period distribution dynamically. Utilizing this distribution in a simple SIR model along with a Bayesian analysis enables policymakers to provide probabilistic warnings about impending surges before they occur. Our methodology is applied to the United Kingdom, where our models successfully predicted the significant Covid-19 surge in July 2021, and also accurately forecasted the minor increases in August and September of that year. Given the promising results from the UK case study, this methodology can be expanded to other countries, and we anticipate improved outcomes by refining the method with longer data sets and incorporating more sophisticated forecasting techniques.

Debugging data problems is a critical challenge in machine learning (ML) pipelines.
Current techniques involve trial-and-error approaches, largely reliant on human intuition,
but these are often inefficient and strain computational resources.
We introduce DataScope, an innovative, efficient, and scalable method for data
validation that identifies issues in large datasets by comparing them with ground
truth or specifications, enabling the isolation of problematic data segments.
Compared to existing methods, DataScope excels in several key areas: it's remarkably
efficient, with speed up to 100x, and it's incredibly scalable, accommodating
datasets and specifications of any size.
Our solution wisely balances the demands of efficiency and accuracy, and it's easy
to integrate, with seamless compatibility with a wide range of data structures
and specifications.

We explore a coordinate ring that incorporates both Cox-Nordgaard and Linström toric ideals, which arises from linear spaces of matrices. By examining this space, we establish a connection between combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. This framework enables us to draw from various fields and offer new insights, such as conditioned randomness results, topological analysis, and enumeration problems with constraints.

The system of three magnetic d-block elements in the form of AB$_3$ type, where A is typically Sc, Y or Lu and B is a 3d or 5d transition metal, has generated significant interest due to the presence of unique magnetic ground states stabilized by a Trimerization phenomenon, most notably in Mn$_3$Sn which is an in-plane antiferromagnet and largest anisotropic ferromagnet known as Helimagnetism. This Trimerization phenomenon leads to the formation of magnetic 'tilted-rotated' states and a related concept 'chiral helix'. This review provides an in-depth analysis of theoretical foundations, experimental investigations and the connections between element-specific properties and the Trimerization-driven unique state evolution in these systems, with a special focus on the design of appropriate magnetic manipulators to access these fragile quantum states and their potential applications in controlling magnetic field-induced multi-fold ground state transitions and other complex phenomena.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have significantly advanced natural language processing capabilities, notably in relation extraction (RE), by facilitating the learning of relevant and high-quality features. However, these advancements come with a significant drawback: the increased demand for substantial training datasets. This paper introduces a new technique to enhance existing datasets, enhancing their quality through a sophisticated annotation method and expansion, thereby improving the performance of relationships identification via a data-rich and diverse set of examples. Our approach to optimizing these annotations leverages computational power, while our method for expanding the dataset effectively reduces the influence of domain-specific factors. This research demonstrates the efficacy of these enhancements on the standard MUC-7 and CBP-2002 datasets, and also introduces a new, highly accurate benchmark on a large, commercially available dataset.

This project seeks to quantify the influence of slight changes in p and r on the initial eigenvalue of a specified spectral problem in terms of its boundary parameter. To accomplish this, we will first establish a precise estimate for how slight changes in p and r impact a particular integral, then use this finding to determine the impact on the eigenvalue. Crucially, our approach employs a particular norm, allowing us to leverage techniques from the calculus of variations to analyze the dependence of these eigenvalues on p and r.

Hypergraphs provide effective models for capturing relationships among subgroups of objects in various fields. However, the inherent complexity of hypergraphs makes the task of extracting their structural characteristics time-consuming. A feasible approach to tackle this issue involves projecting the hypergraphs onto simpler graph representations and analyzing these projections. Nevertheless, the reverse process of hypergraph reconstruction from its projections is an intricate problem, especially in cases where the smallest substructures of the hypergraphs are unknown. This study offers the first comprehensive characterization of the computational hardness of reconstructing hypergraphs from their projections, especially in cases where the smallest substructures are unknown. We investigate the complexity of reconstructing the full hypergraph structure by examining the properties of its projections. Our research reveals that if certain properties of the projections are available for a limited amount of time, the reconstruction task becomes computationally feasible. However, if the smallest substructures of the hypergraphs are unknown, the reconstruction problem becomes computationally hard or even impossible in some cases.

For a physician to confirm the accuracy of imaging results, a specific image detail must be matched with the corresponding description in a medical report. This task, known as visual grounding, is critical but difficult due to the scarcity of annotated data and the complexity of radiological images and reports. To overcome these challenges, we have created the PAXRay dataset, the first collection of images and descriptions from chest X-rays along with precisely localized annotations, and have used it to develop and test advanced models. Unlike existing datasets, which often contain noisy data artifacts and imbalanced classes, the PAXRay dataset is carefully cleaned and includes a balanced class representation, enabling more effective training and evaluation of visual grounding methods.

A notable conjecture suggests that every integral second cohomology class of norm 1 can be formulated as the Euler class of a foliation. Nevertheless, there exist counterexamples for classes of odd degree. Specifically, for every odd number k, there exists a foliation with a Euler class of $H^2$ of norm 1 on $S^1 \times S^{2k+1}$ in the integral cohomology of $S^1 \times S^{2k+1}$. Another conjecture proposes that any integral second cohomology class can be formulated as the Euler class of a compactly oriented foliation with a leaf of maximal volume. However, there exist counterexamples for classes of even degree. Specifically, for every even number k, there exists a foliation with a Euler class of $H^2$ of norm 1 on $S^1 \times S^{2k+1}$ in the integral cohomology of $S^1 \times S^{2k+1}$.

The ability to control the beam angle of emitted light is crucial in many applications, but achieving this with lasers has been difficult due to their inherent characteristics.  Until now, it has not been possible to manipulate the angle of emission in Er doped glass lasers, with the beam typically emerging within a narrow, forward cone. Our research demonstrates the capability to control the angle of emission from Er doped glass lasers, with the possibility of targeting specific directions.  This breakthrough achieves this feat without sacrificing the ability to select the wavelength of emitted light and with minimal degradation.  Our findings provide a foundation for developing techniques to control the direction of emission and also highlight potential avenues for future research and applications.

This study investigates the dynamics of cryptocurrency price pairs using the same analytical methods employed in commodity price research.
Results indicate a shift from negative to positive correlations in later years, characterized by significant peaks and valleys.
Additionally, the study finds considerable variability in coin pairing outcomes, highlighting the need for further research to clarify the underlying mechanisms at play.
Consequently, these findings could influence investment decisions, increasing the need for thorough assessment when assessing alternative digital investments.

This research is motivated by the analogous relationship between the weak noise theory approach, which linearizes the non-linear KPZ equation under moderate noise, and the method of hydrodynamic rescaling, which linearizes the non-linear hydrodynamic equation. The goal of this work is to develop a weak noise transformation that directly applies to the KPZ equation without the need to convert it into a linearized hydrodynamic model. The main contribution of this study is to prove the existence of such a transformation for any dimension within $d$, where the condition $d < 3/2$ holds. The novelty of our findings lies in establishing a weak noise theory framework that accommodates fractional Brownian motion with any Hurwitz coefficient within the range $(1/3, 1/2]$. Additionally, the large-deviation rate function of the KPZ equation is analyzed, and it is shown that this rate function aligns with the solution of an associated nonlinear integral equation. Furthermore, the study also provides a detailed analysis of the regularity properties of the fractional Brownian motion and offers an alternative method for linearizing the non-linear KPZ equation under strong noise conditions.

This paper reviews the key findings from the Magnetospheres mission's FPIC instrument, offering an inside look at the instrument's functioning and scientific results. The Fast Plasma Investigation with Capabilities instrument, specifically designed for its low power consumption, utilized two different measurement methods: a single plasma spectrometer and a spacecraft-built electrostatic analyzer. The former gathered in situ plasma data, while the latter provided insights into the solar wind's electric field. This unique combination enabled scientists to analyze not only the solar wind's magnetic field but also its turbulent plasma patterns and the associated electric forces. The resulting data enabled them to examine the link between these two types of turbulence, as the research indicates, and find evidence supporting the connection between plasma and magnetic field turbulence.

To create extremely short wavelengths using field-synchronized optical cavities, chirp and tuning schemes are employed. This research investigates the effects of a novel chirp and tuning strategy, known as the dynamic top-down chirp-taper scheme, on generating optical cavities. By adjusting the gain-medium lifetime and the cavity's linear detuning, this scheme successfully produces short, stable optical cavities. Our simulations also show that this scheme can create a single, short optical cavity. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that each cavity can produce a strong, coherent X-ray pulse with high stability. Compared to a static top-down scheme, the dynamic top-down chirp-taper scheme offers shorter pulse durations and increased pulse stability. This improved scheme can lead to higher average powers and a greater number of pulses within a given time frame, thereby enhancing the overall pulse density.

Starting from the linearized Euler equations for stratified inviscid compressible fluids, we derive a modified Taylor-Goldstein equation by simplifying assumptions common in geophysical flows. The new equation incorporates vertical velocity perturbations in its derivation, unlike the traditional Taylor-Goldstein equation derived under hydrostatic and quasi-hydrostatic assumptions. The validity of the derived equation is discussed through comparing energy equations for quasi-hydrostatic and internal gravity waves.

Creating and evaluating district maps is a complex task. Various groups use different criteria to develop maps that serve their specific needs, yet a universal framework for comparing them is lacking. In our study, we develop a framework for assessing the fairness of multiple district plans simultaneously, employing Simulated Annealing to optimize a fairness metric that leverages both the MaxCut and fairness metrics. By allowing for the automatic generation of fair maps and combining human and machine judgments, our approach facilitates a more collaborative and engaging redistricting process.

The process of recognizing and categorizing defects in fabric images can be challenging due to the intricate and varied nature of the fabric background. To effectively isolate the defect information from the background and facilitate recognition, this study proposes an innovative method that decomposes a single-color channel image into separate foreground and background components. By repeatedly applying low-rank decomposition to the foreground with increasingly strict regularization, the algorithm systematically remove any background presence from the components, ultimately extracting the pure defect information. The separation of background and defects is then straightforward. Notably, this method is highly adaptable and can be applied to various datasets without the need for extensive tuning. Experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple datasets.

An intelligent agent capable of independent movement navigates a mysterious environment, relying on top-down guidance and sensory input from bottom-up sensors. Following independent actions, the newly observed visual data provides additional insights. The agent's policy is designed to maximize the mutual influence between its navigation actions and observed visuals by learning a correlation that utilizes all past experience. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning approaches which focus on maximizing long-term rewards, our method focuses on learning a meaningful connection between related observations and actions, without relying on external reward structures. The resulting policy enables the agent to make the most informed navigation decisions and achieve a higher level of observation consistency. Experimental evaluations on multiple environments confirm that our approach produces more consistent observations and significantly reduces navigation errors.

Investigating Brans-Dicke theory, we focus on a specific model where the metric conforms to the Robin boundary condition at spatial infinity. Crucially, for photons to reach null infinity, a particular integral of the Brans-Dicke field, $W(r)$, must meet specific criteria at spatial infinity. If $W(r)$ meets this requirement, a global solution, $B_{\rm ext}(t,r)$, exists, satisfying the Robin problem and corresponding equations, including the Brans-Dicke field equation and the Einstein and Brans-Dicke field equations, and this scenario is applicable to any static black hole. A key finding arises in the form of a non-trivial global representation of the metric and Brans-Dicke field for any static black hole, including the Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstr\"om metrics. Furthermore, a corresponding analysis for the Einstein gamma-Newton and Brans-Dicke gamma-Newton gravities is also presented.

We introduce the first population III binary merger rate model based on a population synthesis framework, accounting for the formation of the initial binary system through a critical stellar mass threshold and binary separation limit. The population III binary merger rate peaks at a significant $z$, with approximately $1.7\times10^{-8}$ yr$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-3}$ at $z\sim15$. Considering a limited binary fraction and low-mass cutoff, our derived merger rate of Population III binary remnants in a specific mass range aligns with findings from gravitational wave observations, suggesting that a significant portion of these events can be attributed to the fragmentation of primordial gas. Additionally, we project that the forthcoming Roman telescope will likely detect no more than three Population III binary mergers within a year.

Identifying incidents in distribution grids promptly is crucial for minimizing disruptions in power supply. Traditional incident detection algorithms rely on explicit meter data connections; nonetheless, such configurations can be challenging and costly in modern distribution grids featuring energy storage systems and internet of things devices. This research proposes a data-driven incident detection method that processes pre-processed data from an information market without a central hub, showing its effectiveness on real-world datasets.

The intermediate mesons $\rho$ and $\omega$ produced in the X(3872)'s decay to $J/\psi$ via virtual photons are examined. Decays involving an additional photon are considered, in addition to the case where this photon is absent, allowing for a direct comparison of the contributions made by the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons. Calculations of branching ratios for X(3872) decays to $J/\psi$ $\pi$ $\pi$ and $J/\psi$ $\pi$ $\pi$ $\gamma$ are provided, taking into account the influence of off-shell mesons and the underlying hadronic currents. A comparison of the branching ratios for different decay channels, specifically $J/\psi$ $\pi$ $\pi$ and $J/\psi$ $\pi$ $\pi$ $\gamma$, is also presented, in order to assess the feasibility of detecting the X(3872) at facilities such as BESIII, BELLEII, and LHCb.

A comprehensive and detailed analysis of smooth quadrics is provided with a focus on their classification, theoretical foundations, core attributes, defined sets, embedding techniques, boundary characterization, specific quadric type classification, and a comprehensive diagram illustrating relationships between these classifications.

The advancement of machine learning in the gaming sector has been accelerated by the open-source TextWorld framework, which enables large-scale simulations of text-based games to be conducted easily. Nevertheless, the slow throughput of these simulations has been a major constraint for researchers. In response to this challenge, we introduce TextWorldExpress, a novel automated testing tool that enhances the throughput of text game simulations by leveraging a combination of advanced techniques, including AI-powered playing agents and pre-processing methods. With Express, the entire testing cycle, including setup, game playing, and assessment, is accomplished within 200 microseconds per game. Moreover, our tool requires minimal configuration and supports a wide range of testing scenarios, making it suitable for large-scale integration in automated testing environments.

In three-dimensional Topological Insulators, the presence of point defects such as vacancies and interstitials can divert electron paths in the bulk within voids or around dislocations. The influence of line defects, specifically edge dislocations, on electron behavior beyond their point counterparts needs to be investigated. The edge dislocation serves as a source of strain, altering the electronic band structure and transport properties. Utilizing the Green's function method in conjunction with the Kubo formula allows us to calculate both local and bulk conductivity in the presence of imperfections. Applying this theoretical framework to a well-studied 3D Topological Insulator model, our findings indicate that dislocations can create pathways for electron tunneling across gaps within the bulk, influencing the overall conductivity and thermal conductivity. The calculated conductivities take into account the strain caused by dislocations, with tunable scattering lengths influencing transition between insulating and topological phases.

This note builds upon a previous work by Figueroa and Manfredi to explore the uniqueness of positive $p$-harmonic functions within specific domains, particularly those with non-convex boundaries and featuring angular points. Uniqueness is demonstrated for a wide range of $p$-harmonic functions under the condition that $p > 1$. The influence of the parameter $p$ on the uniqueness of these functions is also examined. Moreover, this note attempts to provide insight into the lower limit of the uniqueness range for $p$.

Using a large dataset from the Metop satellite, we investigated the largest weather occurrences on the globe and their relationship to each other over long distances. Focusing on wind speeds above 40ms^-1, we found that when extreme wind speeds occur at one location, there is a significant probability of similar wind speeds occurring at other locations within a certain distance. This probability gradually decreases as the distance increases, with an approximate decay rate of 10km for wind speeds and 500km for wave heights. This pattern held true for analyses on different timescales, from hours to 10 days. This research provides new insights into the link between extreme weather occurrences and their spatial relationships.
